summary: A small exchange of June 1899: Wilde asking the journalist W. Morton Fullerton for a hundred francs under his assumed name, and Fullerton's reply — his own words, which few people on this map get.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote:
My dear Fullerton, I find myself in very great trouble owing to not getting some money I expected, from America, where it is owing to me.

Would it be an inconvenience to you to lend me 100 francs? I receive my quarterly allowance, such as it is, on July 1st, when I will be able to return it to you. At present I am quite without money, and I hope you will not mind my asking you this favour.

If you are able to do this would you send it to me, Monsieur _Sebastian Melmoth_, at the above address? Believe me, truly yours

OSCAR WILDE
sources.context: Wilde to W. Morton Fullerton, [June 1899], Hotel Marsollier (MS Harvard) - quoted whole. 'Sebastian Melmoth' is underlined in the original: the money has to be addressed to the alias, which is the exile's whole condition in one clause. Eighteen months before his death.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: Wilde asking a journalist for a hundred francs, under his assumed name.

sources.quote: My dear Melmoth, I am distressed to have left your touching appeal unanswered for so long. But I have been on conge in the patrie of Stendhal, and had cognisance of your gene only yesterday.
sources.context: Fullerton's reply, 3 June 1899, 35 boulevard des Capucines (MS Clark), quoted by the editors. His own words, which few people on this map get. He addresses Wilde by the alias without remark - 'My dear Melmoth' - which is what the courtesy of that circle looked like in practice. 'conge' is leave; 'gene' is embarrassment or want.
sources.speaker: W. Morton Fullerton
sources.supports: That the appeal was answered, and how Fullerton addressed him.
